Test your knowledge of the material on [correspondence analysis](../lectures/05-Corresp.pdf) in the following quiz to see how much you learned.
This is **entirely private for you**---no records are kept of your performance. When you've answered all the questions, click on the Submit Quiz button
to see how you've done, and perhaps get pointers to things you should review.

<div class="quiz-container">

<form id="quizForm">

<div class="question" id="q1">
<h3>1. Correspondence analysis (CA) is best described as:</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="a" id="q1a"> <label for="q1a">a) The analog of principal component analysis (PCA) for frequency data</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="b" id="q1b"> <label for="q1b">b) A chi-square test for independence in contingency tables</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="c" id="q1c"> <label for="q1c">c) A regression method for categorical predictors</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q1" value="d" id="q1d"> <label for="q1d">d) A clustering algorithm for categorical data</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp1"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q2">
<h3>2. Correspondence analysis uses which mathematical technique to find optimal row and column scores?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="a" id="q2a"> <label for="q2a">a) Maximum likelihood estimation</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="b" id="q2b"> <label for="q2b">b) Singular value decomposition (SVD) of residuals from independence</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="c" id="q2c"> <label for="q2c">c) Iterative proportional fitting</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q2" value="d" id="q2d"> <label for="q2d">d) Principal component analysis</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp2"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q3">
<h3>3. The singular values (λ<sub>i</sub>) in correspondence analysis represent:</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="a" id="q3a"> <label for="q3a">a) The variances of the principal components</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="b" id="q3b"> <label for="q3b">b) The correlations between row and column category scores on each dimension</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="c" id="q3c"> <label for="q3c">c) The chi-square statistics for each dimension</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q3" value="d" id="q3d"> <label for="q3d">d) The eigenvalues of the contingency table</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp3"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q4">
<h3>4. For a two-way contingency table with <em>r</em> rows and <em>c</em> columns, the CA solution has at most how many dimensions?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="a" id="q4a"> <label for="q4a">a) <em>r</em> + <em>c</em></label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="b" id="q4b"> <label for="q4b">b) <em>r</em> × <em>c</em></label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="c" id="q4c"> <label for="q4c">c) min(<em>r</em> - 1, <em>c</em> - 1)</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q4" value="d" id="q4d"> <label for="q4d">d) max(<em>r</em>, <em>c</em>)</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp4"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q5">
<h3>5. How does the Pearson chi-square statistic (χ²) relate to the inertia in CA?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="a" id="q5a"> <label for="q5a">a) χ² = <em>n</em> × Σλ²<sub>i</sub>, where <em>n</em> is the sample size and λ<sub>i</sub> are the singular values</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="b" id="q5b"> <label for="q5b">b) χ² = Σλ<sub>i</sub>, the sum of singular values</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="c" id="q5c"> <label for="q5c">c) χ² = <em>n</em> × λ<sub>1</sub>, where λ<sub>1</sub> is the first singular value</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q5" value="d" id="q5d"> <label for="q5d">d) There is no relationship between χ² and inertia</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp5"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q6">
<h3>6. What does the term "inertia" mean in correspondence analysis?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="a" id="q6a"> <label for="q6a">a) The total sample size in the contingency table</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="b" id="q6b"> <label for="q6b">b) The weighted variation or dispersion of row/column profiles from the centroid</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="c" id="q6c"> <label for="q6c">c) The number of dimensions needed for the analysis</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q6" value="d" id="q6d"> <label for="q6d">d) The correlation between rows and columns</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp6"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q7">
<h3>7. In the default "symmetric" CA map, what does it mean when a row point and column point are plotted near each other?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="a" id="q7a"> <label for="q7a">a) They have a positive association (residual from independence > 0)</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="b" id="q7b"> <label for="q7b">b) They are independent</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="c" id="q7c"> <label for="q7c">c) They have a negative association</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q7" value="d" id="q7d"> <label for="q7d">d) They have equal marginal frequencies</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp7"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q8">
<h3>8. Which of the following is TRUE about CA solutions?</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="a" id="q8a"> <label for="q8a">a) CA solutions are nested, similar to PCA (the first two dimensions of a 3D solution are identical to the 2D solution)</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="b" id="q8b"> <label for="q8b">b) The centroid of row and column profiles is located at a corner of the plot</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="c" id="q8c"> <label for="q8c">c) Distances in a CA plot use Euclidean distance, not chi-square distance</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q8" value="d" id="q8d"> <label for="q8d">d) Different dimensions from a CA solution can be freely rotated like in factor analysis</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp8"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q9">
<h3>9. Multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) differs from simple CA in that MCA:</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q9" value="a" id="q9a"> <label for="q9a">a) Analyzes all pairwise bivariate associations among multiple categorical variables</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q9" value="b" id="q9b"> <label for="q9b">b) Can only be used for binary variables</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q9" value="c" id="q9c"> <label for="q9c">c) Uses a different mathematical technique than SVD</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q9" value="d" id="q9d"> <label for="q9d">d) Cannot display all variables in a single plot</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp9"></div>
</div>

<div class="question" id="q10">
<h3>10. For MCA with <em>Q</em> categorical variables, the Burt matrix is:</h3>
<div class="options">
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q10" value="a" id="q10a"> <label for="q10a">a) A matrix of dummy variables with 0s and 1s</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q10" value="b" id="q10b"> <label for="q10b">b) The product of the indicator matrix <strong>Z</strong> and its transpose, <strong>B</strong> = <strong>Z</strong><sup>T</sup><strong>Z</strong></label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q10" value="c" id="q10c"> <label for="q10c">c) The original contingency table</label></div>
<div class="option"><input type="radio" name="q10" value="d" id="q10d"> <label for="q10d">d) A diagonal matrix of singular values</label></div>
</div>
<div class="explanation" id="exp10"></div>
</div>

<button type="button" class="submit-btn" onclick="gradeQuiz()">Submit Quiz</button>
<button type="button" class="reset-btn" onclick="resetQuiz()">Reset Quiz</button>

</form>

<div class="score-summary" id="scoreSummary"></div>

</div>

<script>
// Correct answers
const answers = {
  q1: 'a',
  q2: 'b',
  q3: 'b',
  q4: 'c',
  q5: 'a',
  q6: 'b',
  q7: 'a',
  q8: 'a',
  q9: 'a',
  q10: 'b'
};

// Explanations for each question
const explanations = {
  q1: {
    correct: "CA is the analog of PCA for frequency data. Like PCA, it aims to account for the maximum amount of variation (χ² in this case) in a few dimensions and provides optimal scaling of row and column categories.",
    incorrect: "CA is specifically designed as the analog of principal component analysis (PCA) for frequency data in contingency tables. While it uses χ² to measure association, it's not just a chi-square test—it's a dimension reduction and visualization technique."
  },
  q2: {
    correct: "CA uses singular value decomposition (SVD) of the matrix of residuals from independence. This decomposes the residuals as D = XΛY<sup>T</sup>, where X and Y are the row and column scores, and Λ contains the singular values.",
    incorrect: "The key mathematical technique in CA is singular value decomposition (SVD) applied to the residuals from independence. This provides the optimal scaling of category scores that maximizes their correlation on each dimension."
  },
  q3: {
    correct: "The singular values λ<sub>i</sub> are the (canonical) correlations between the row and column category scores on each dimension. For dimension 1, the scores are chosen to have the maximum possible correlation λ<sub>1</sub>, and so on for subsequent dimensions.",
    incorrect: "The singular values in CA represent the correlations between row and column category scores. This is the 'optimal scaling' interpretation of CA—each pair of scores has the highest possible correlation (= λ<sub>m</sub>) for that dimension."
  },
  q4: {
    correct: "The CA solution has at most min(r - 1, c - 1) dimensions. This is the rank of the matrix of residuals from independence, similar to how PCA has at most min(n - 1, p) dimensions for n observations and p variables.",
    incorrect: "The maximum number of dimensions in CA is min(r - 1, c - 1), where r is the number of rows and c is the number of columns. For example, a 4×4 table has at most 3 dimensions, and a 6×4 table has at most 3 dimensions."
  },
  q5: {
    correct: "The Pearson χ² statistic equals n times the sum of squared singular values: χ² = n × Σλ²<sub>i</sub>. The total inertia is Σλ²<sub>i</sub> = χ²/n, so the percentage of inertia explained by each dimension reflects the percentage of χ² accounted for.",
    incorrect: "The relationship is χ² = n × Σλ²<sub>i</sub>, where n is the sample size. The total inertia (Σλ²<sub>i</sub>) equals χ²/n. This is why we can interpret the % inertia accounted for by each dimension as the % of χ² explained."
  },
  q6: {
    correct: "Inertia refers to the weighted variation or dispersion of the profile points from their centroid (weighted average). The physical analogy is to mass × distance², hence the term 'inertia.' Higher inertia indicates greater association between rows and columns.",
    incorrect: "Inertia is the weighted variation of row/column profiles from the centroid. It measures the dispersion of profile points, with weights based on marginal frequencies (mass). The squared distance from the centroid, weighted by mass, gives the contribution to inertia."
  },
  q7: {
    correct: "In a symmetric CA map, when a row point and column point are near each other, it indicates a positive association between them—the residual from independence (d<sub>ij</sub>) is positive. Proximity reflects similarity or attraction in the data.",
    incorrect: "Proximity in a CA plot indicates positive association. When row point i and column point j are close together, the observed frequency exceeds what would be expected under independence (positive residual). This is a key interpretive principle of CA plots."
  },
  q8: {
    correct: "CA solutions are nested, just like PCA. The first two dimensions of a 3D solution are identical to the 2D solution. Additionally, the centroid (weighted average) of row and column profiles is at the origin, and distances reflect chi-square distances.",
    incorrect: "CA solutions are nested, meaning you can extract lower-dimensional solutions from higher-dimensional ones without recomputing. The centroids are at the origin (not at corners), distances are chi-square distances (not Euclidean), and dimensions cannot be freely rotated."
  },
  q9: {
    correct: "MCA extends CA to n-way tables and analyzes all pairwise bivariate associations among the categorical variables. It can plot all factors in a single display and provides an optimal scaling of category scores across all variables simultaneously.",
    incorrect: "MCA (multiple correspondence analysis) analyzes all pairwise bivariate associations among multiple categorical variables. It works with the indicator matrix (or Burt matrix) and can display all variables in a single plot, providing a comprehensive view of associations."
  },
  q10: {
    correct: "The Burt matrix is B = Z<sup>T</sup>Z, the product of the indicator matrix Z and its transpose. The diagonal blocks contain marginal frequencies for each variable, and the off-diagonal blocks contain the bivariate contingency tables for each pair of variables.",
    incorrect: "The Burt matrix is defined as B = Z<sup>T</sup>Z. For two categorical variables, it's a symmetric matrix with marginal frequencies on the diagonal blocks and the contingency table N in the off-diagonal blocks. MCA can be performed on the Burt matrix."
  }
};
</script>
